summary:
Virginia is a state in the United States, and the exposures a trans visitor is most likely to meet are set at national level. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to 'correct the misapplication' of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). Several federal measures adopted since have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any single measure should be checked before travel.

Travel documents are the sharpest practical risk. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a departmental policy in place since 1992, and litigation brought by the ACLU on behalf of seven plaintiffs continues in federal courts. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening adds a second document exposure. After the executive order of 5 February 2025 titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', the State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth.

Checkpoint procedures carry an outing risk of their own. Transportation Security Administration screening involves secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk exposing a trans traveller's status during the process.

The federal bar on trans people using government-funded single-sex facilities applies in Virginia's federally funded buildings. At state level, the sources record a 2014 Gloucester County case in which a transgender high school student was denied use of the boys' bathroom and the school board was ruled to have acted unlawfully; the U.S. Supreme Court let that outcome stand in 2021. The same sources record a July 2023 federal Department of Education policy barring bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender individuals in schools, with reversal intended in 2026.

A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Virginia in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, and names Virginia with Arizona as a state that enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies that, because of state-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

Virginia's own statutory baseline is protective for adults. The Virginia Values Act, passed 6 February 2020 and signed 11 April 2020, prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit from 1 July 2020, replacing the earlier state-employment-only protections, and a 4 March 2020 law allows localities to enact their own protections on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Violence against trans people has statutory standing. Virginia hate crime laws address violence based on gender identity under a bill signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, and HB 2132 repealing the gay and trans panic defence was passed in March 2021, signed by Governor Northam and in force from 1 July 2021.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 September 2020 changing sex on a Virginia birth certificate has required only 'appropriate clinical treatment' rather than the sex reassignment surgery required from 1979, and since 1 July 2020 Virginia has offered an 'X' gender marker on driver's licences. Neither state provision alters the federal passport position described above, which governs international travel.

Sport and youth policy are where Virginia's restrictions sit. In February 2025 the Virginia High School League banned transgender athletes from girls' sports following the president's executive order, and Virginia prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of minors. Federal care restrictions apply alongside this: Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation, the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19, and proposed health-department rules of October 2025 would bar Medicaid reimbursement for such care to patients under 18.

Relationship recognition is settled in statute for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 6 October 2014 after the Supreme Court refused appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer, the defunct statutory ban was repealed 3 March 2020, and a codifying protection signed in March 2024 took effect 1 July 2024.

Federal custody remains a documented site of harm if a trans visitor is detained. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates mandating short hair, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them 'like a man', with beatings and solitary confinement for those who refused, alongside widely reported severe sexual abuse.
tangentialFactors:
The comparison group matters for expectations on the ground. Virginia sits with Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia in a July 2026 assessment's low-risk tier, but the same assessment singles out Virginia and Arizona as states that enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on state-specific factors, appear unlikely to spread to adults. Youth measures are the pattern: the February 2025 high-school sports ban, the standing prohibition on providers attempting to change a minor's gender identity, and school-facility litigation beginning with the 2014 Gloucester County case.

Official signals in Virginia run in both directions. The Virginia Supreme Court upheld reinstatement in September 2021 of a teacher suspended for refusing to use a transgender child's pronouns on Christian-belief grounds, and Governor Youngkin vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity in May 2024. Set against those, the 2020 legislative wave (non-discrimination, hate crime, local authority, the X marker, birth-certificate reform) and the 2021 panic-defence repeal give trans residents and visitors a statutory footing that several other states have withdrawn.

Federal turbulence is the larger variable. The military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth are all in force or in litigation, and several have been blocked or enjoined. Enforcement posture has also hardened at national level: in December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, and a May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

A cross-state template is under discussion. Rights groups described the March 2026 Kansas law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth as a model for other state legislatures, with further targeting bills pending elsewhere; Virginia's current document rules do not follow that model, but the assessment's low-risk designation is dated July 2026 and rests on the state-specific factors that have so far contained youth measures.
localsOnly:
Virginia's non-discrimination statute covers gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit from 1 July 2020, and the 4 March 2020 law lets cities and counties adopt their own protections on sexual orientation and gender identity, so the practical level of protection varies by locality within the state.

For residents, changing sex on a birth certificate requires 'appropriate clinical treatment' only, from 1 September 2020, without the surgery requirement that applied from 1979, and driver's licences carry an 'X' gender marker from 1 July 2020. Hate crime liability covers gender identity, and the gay and trans panic defence was repealed by HB 2132 in March 2021, in force 1 July 2021.

Health care for minors is restricted: Virginia prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of minors, and federal restrictions described in the summary apply to facilities operating under federal rules or funding.

Adoption and family law carry religious exemptions. HB 189 and SB 349, signed 9 April 2012 and effective 1 July 2012, authorise adoption agencies to refuse placements for religious reasons, while a February 2021 bill barred taxpayer money going to religious organisations that discriminate in adoption. Surrogacy contracts for same-sex couples were legalised by a bill passed February 2019, signed March 2019 and effective 1 July 2019.

Other resident-facing measures include SB 1138, decriminalising and modernising HIV laws, signed 31 March 2021, and a PrEP insurance anti-discrimination bill vetoed in March 2025. Hospital visitation rights for same-sex couples were established by a designated visitor statute signed 26 March 2007, effective 1 July 2007.
outOfScopeNotes:
Virginia's own statewide position on trans people's use of public bathrooms and facilities is not established by the sources supplied. The research dossier relies on a Movement Advancement Project equality map for its state-by-state list of facility bans, and the URL cited for that map returns HTTP 404, the page having moved; the ban status recorded there for Virginia is therefore unresolved.

The status of the 2006 Virginia constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage is unresolved. Repeal resolutions were approved in January 2025 and January 2026 for a voter referendum, and the sources do not state whether the referendum has been held or the amendment removed, while the statutory layer is repealed and a codifying protection has been in force since 1 July 2024.

Which federal measures are operative on any given date is unresolved. Several of the orders and rules listed here have been blocked or enjoined, and the passport litigation described as continuing in federal courts was still open at the time of the July 2026 assessment.

The characterisation of the July 2023 Department of Education policy and of its intended 2026 reversal is taken from a single secondary source and is not independently verified in this record.

Items in the source inventory with no trans bearing have been excluded as out of scope: the invalidation of Virginia's sodomy and crimes-against-nature statutes by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003 and the 2013-2014 repeals of lewd cohabitation and fornication provisions, the 1991 ruling in French Quarter Cafe v. Virginia Alcoholic Beverage Control Board striking the 1934 ban on gay bars, and an archaic Code reference defining homosexuality as sexual conduct discovered in August 2022. The evidentiary base for the Virginia entries is an encyclopaedia article plus a July 2026 third-party legal risk assessment rather than primary legislative text.
